whoIsThisFor.heading: Who is the UX Designer exam for?

personas.label: Designers working on Salesforce projects
personas.description: You know UX practice already and need the platform half: SLDS, Lightning App Builder, what can actually be changed and what cannot.

personas.label: Admins who have become the de facto designer
personas.description: Nobody else is deciding how the pages look, so you are. This covers the research and accessibility vocabulary to back up those decisions.

personas.label: Product designers moving into enterprise software
personas.description: Consumer design instincts need adjusting for a platform where users spend eight hours a day and the component library is fixed.

examDifficulty.heading: Is the UX Designer Exam Hard?
examDifficulty.summary: Moderate, and awkward in a specific way: it tests two bodies of knowledge that rarely sit in the same head. One half is design practice, research methods, design thinking, WCAG. The other half is Salesforce configuration, SLDS, App Builder, Dynamic Forms. Designers tend to lose marks on the second; admins on the first.
bullets: 60 questions in 105 minutes. No code to read, so time is rarely the binding constraint.
Around 65% to pass, which leaves room for roughly 21 wrong.
Design thinking phases get asked directly. A question describes an activity and wants to know whether it belongs to Empathise, Define, Ideate, Prototype or Test.
Accessibility is specific, not general. WCAG 2.1 AA, the four POUR principles, and the actual contrast ratio of 4.5:1 for body text.
examDifficulty.passRateGuidance: Two checks before booking. Can you name a research method appropriate to a question you are handed, and say what it will and will not tell you? And can you look at a page requirement and say whether Dynamic Forms, a compact layout, or neither is the answer? Those two cover most of what the exam does.

examFormat.heading: UX Designer Exam Format Explained
examFormat.intro: Proctored online or at a test centre. The shape of it:
examFormat.scenarioPercent: Around half the questions describe a situation. Three patterns recur: pick the research method for a stated question, identify which accessibility principle a problem breaches, and choose the Salesforce feature that satisfies a page requirement.
bestWayToPass: Learn the phases by their outputs. Interviews and journey maps belong to Empathise, a problem statement to Define, sketches to Ideate, and so on. When a question describes an artefact, the phase follows from it.
Treat WCAG as facts to know, not principles to grasp. The contrast ratios, what a text alternative is for, keyboard operability. These are the questions you either get or do not.
Open Lightning App Builder and change something. Add a Dynamic Form, put a visibility rule on a field, edit a compact layout. The feature names stick once you have used them.
Separate qualitative from quantitative. Interviews and usability tests tell you why; surveys and analytics tell you how many. Several questions hinge only on that split.

certificationCard.description: This exam covers user research, wireframing and prototyping, accessibility to WCAG 2.1 AA, and the Salesforce tools you use to apply them: the Lightning Design System, Lightning App Builder, Dynamic Forms and Experience Cloud.

keyConcepts.h2: UX Designer: Key Concepts for the Exam

blocks.heading: The Five Phases of Design Thinking
blocks.body: Empathise, Define, Ideate, Prototype, Test. The exam treats these as a vocabulary you need rather than a philosophy, and the fastest route in is through what each phase produces. Empathise produces research: interviews, observation, journey maps, personas. Define narrows that into a problem statement, often written as a point of view or a how-might-we question. Ideate produces options, sketches, crazy eights, affinity diagrams, with the rule that quantity precedes judgement. Prototype produces something a person can react to, from a paper sketch to a clickable mock. Test puts it in front of users and produces findings that send you back round. The phases are iterative rather than a sequence you finish, and questions sometimes check that you know going backwards is normal.

blocks.heading: Choosing a Research Method
blocks.body: The most common scenario on this exam hands you a question and asks which method answers it. Qualitative methods explain reasons: interviews surface motivations, contextual inquiry shows what people actually do rather than what they report, usability testing reveals where a design fails and why, with five to eight participants typically enough to find the recurring problems. Quantitative methods measure scale: surveys tell you how widespread an attitude is, analytics show real behaviour at volume, task completion rates and time on task give you a number to compare against. Two specialist methods come up by name. Card sorting asks users to group content and tells you how they expect information to be organised. Tree testing takes a structure you already have and checks whether people can find things in it. Sorting builds the structure, testing validates it.

blocks.heading: Wireframes, Prototypes and Handoff
blocks.body: These sit on a ladder of fidelity, and the exam cares about matching the rung to the purpose. A sketch or low-fidelity wireframe is for agreeing layout and hierarchy cheaply, and its roughness is useful because people criticise it freely. A high-fidelity mock carries real colour, type and spacing and is what you use to agree the visual design. An interactive prototype is for testing flow, where the question is whether someone can get through a task rather than whether a button is the right blue. Handoff to an admin or developer needs more than pictures: the states a component takes, what happens when data is missing or a list is empty, error and validation behaviour, and the responsive rules. Designs that only show the happy path are the ones that get built wrong.

blocks.heading: Accessibility: WCAG 2.1 and SLDS
blocks.body: WCAG organises everything under four principles, POUR. Perceivable means it can be sensed: text alternatives for images, captions for media, and contrast of at least 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text. Operable means it can be driven: every interactive element reachable and usable by keyboard, with a visible focus indicator, and no reliance on a mouse or on precise timing. Understandable means it behaves predictably: consistent navigation, clear labels, errors that explain how to fix them. Robust means it works with assistive technology: valid markup and correct ARIA roles and names. The Lightning Design System matters here because its components already meet much of this, which is why building with SLDS and respecting its markup is usually the accessible answer and hand-rolled custom markup usually is not.

blocks.heading: Lightning App Builder, Dynamic Forms and the Tooling
blocks.body: This is the half that catches designers out. Lightning App Builder composes record pages from components, with component visibility rules that show or hide based on field values, device or user. Dynamic Forms breaks the old monolithic page layout into individual fields you can place in any section and make conditional, which is how you keep a long record page from overwhelming users. Dynamic Actions does the same for buttons; surfacing only the actions valid in the current context. Compact layouts control what shows in the record highlights panel and in mobile previews, so they decide what a user sees first. Path guides users through stages with key fields and guidance for success. For the exam, the pattern is a requirement such as showing a field only to a certain profile; or only when a status is set, and the answer is the specific feature designed for it.

scenarioTips.h2: How to Pass the Salesforce UX Designer Exam
scenarioTips.intro: This exam asks you to apply design practice inside a platform with fixed components. The design content is mostly recall; the Salesforce content needs an hour in App Builder.

blocks.heading: Phases by Their Artefacts
blocks.body: Learn which output belongs to which design thinking phase. That mapping answers the phase questions directly.

blocks.heading: WCAG Numbers
blocks.body: 4.5:1 for normal text, 3:1 for large text, keyboard operability, visible focus, text alternatives. Memorise them; they are asked as facts.

blocks.heading: Qualitative or Quantitative
blocks.body: Interviews and usability tests explain why. Surveys and analytics measure how many. Most method questions turn on this one distinction.

blocks.heading: Card Sorting Versus Tree Testing
blocks.body: Sorting discovers how users would organise content. Tree testing checks whether they can navigate a structure you already built.

blocks.heading: Dynamic Forms and Visibility Rules
blocks.body: Go into Lightning App Builder and set a field to appear only when a picklist has a certain value. The feature names are much easier to recall afterwards.

sampleQuestions.question: A team has written a problem statement after three weeks of user interviews. Which design thinking phase have they just completed?
sampleQuestions.explanation: Define is the phase that turns research into a sharply stated problem.
whyWrong: Ideate generates options after the problem is defined.
Testing validates a prototype, which does not exist yet.
Empathise is the research itself, which came before the statement.

sampleQuestions.question: A designer needs to know whether users can find a policy document in the existing navigation. Which method fits?
sampleQuestions.explanation: Tree testing checks findability within a structure that already exists.
whyWrong: A/B testing compares two variants, which is not the question here.
A survey captures opinion, not whether someone can navigate.
Card sorting discovers how users would group content, which is useful when building a structure rather than checking one.

sampleQuestions.question: Body text on a custom component is mid-grey on white at a contrast ratio of 3.2:1. Which WCAG 2.1 AA requirement does this fail?
options: Perceivable, because normal text needs at least 4.5:1
Robust, because grey is simply not a valid colour value
Operable, because the text cannot be clicked
sampleQuestions.explanation: Contrast minimums sit under Perceivable, and normal-size text requires 4.5:1.
whyWrong: Understandable concerns predictability and clarity of language and behaviour.
Robust concerns compatibility with assistive technology.
Operable concerns keyboard and input, not contrast.

sampleQuestions.question: A record page must show a Reason for Discount field only when the Discount field is above zero. What satisfies this?
options: Dynamic Forms with a field visibility rule
A validation rule placed onto the object
sampleQuestions.explanation: Dynamic Forms allows per-field placement and conditional visibility based on field values.
whyWrong: Compact layouts control the highlights panel, not conditional display in the form.
Record types are a heavier structural change than this requirement needs.
A validation rule enforces data entry; it does not hide a field.

sampleQuestions.question: A product owner asks why users abandon a multi-step form. Which approach will answer that?
options: Moderated usability testing with a small number of users
A satisfaction survey sent out to every single one of the users
sampleQuestions.explanation: Watching people attempt the task shows where and why they stop, which is a qualitative question.
whyWrong: Analytics show that abandonment happens without explaining the cause.
Ticket volume is an indirect signal and only captures people who complained.
A survey measures attitude at scale but rarely explains a specific failure point.

sampleQuestions.question: Which WCAG principle is breached when a dropdown can only be opened with a mouse?
sampleQuestions.explanation: Operable covers keyboard access and input independence.
whyWrong: Understandable is about predictable behaviour and clear language.
Perceivable is about whether content can be sensed, such as contrast and text alternatives.
Robust is about compatibility with assistive technology.

sampleQuestions.question: Why is building with Lightning Design System components usually the more accessible choice?
options: They load a great deal faster than any hand-written custom markup does
They already implement much of the required markup, focus handling and ARIA
sampleQuestions.explanation: SLDS components are built to meet accessibility requirements, so using them inherits that work.
whyWrong: Performance is a separate concern from accessibility.
SLDS components can be themed and extended.
Nothing bypasses WCAG; SLDS helps you meet it.

sampleQuestions.question: A stakeholder wants to agree on page layout and hierarchy before any visual design work. What should the designer produce?
options: A clickable prototype with final content
sampleQuestions.explanation: Low fidelity keeps the conversation on structure, and its roughness invites honest criticism.
whyWrong: A document alone makes layout hard to evaluate.
An interactive prototype is for testing flow, which is a later question.
High fidelity moves the discussion to colour and type too early.

sampleQuestions.question: What does card sorting tell a designer?
options: How many users prefer a given colour
How users expect content to be grouped and labelled
Whether a given page meets the contrast requirements
sampleQuestions.explanation: Card sorting surfaces the user's own mental model of how information belongs together.
whyWrong: Usability is established by testing a prototype with tasks.
Preference at scale is a survey question.
Contrast is measured, not sorted.

sampleQuestions.question: A long record page overwhelms users, and different teams need different fields. What is the appropriate Salesforce response?
options: Dynamic Forms, placing fields in sections with visibility rules
Create an entirely separate custom object for each one of the teams
sampleQuestions.explanation: Dynamic Forms exists for exactly this: breaking the layout into fields that appear conditionally.
whyWrong: Separate objects fragment the data model for a presentation problem.
Training around a design problem leaves the design problem in place.
Removing fields other teams rely on solves one problem by creating another.

sampleQuestions.question: Which handoff detail is most often missing and most likely to cause a build to go wrong?
sampleQuestions.explanation: Designs that show only the populated happy path leave the developer to invent the rest.
whyWrong: Rationale is useful context but does not change what gets built.
Typography is usually specified and is rarely the gap.
Competitor research is background, not build detail.

sampleQuestions.question: Roughly how many participants are typically enough for a usability test to surface the recurring problems?
sampleQuestions.explanation: A small number of participants reveals most of the repeat issues, which is why usability testing is cheap to run often.
whyWrong: A single participant cannot show you which problems recur.
Thirty to fifty is the scale of a quantitative study, not a usability test.
Hundreds of participants is survey or analytics territory.

sampleQuestions.question: What does Dynamic Actions control?
options: Which buttons appear, based on record context
The record highlights panel at the top of the page
sampleQuestions.explanation: Dynamic Actions surfaces only the actions valid in context, reducing the clutter of a fixed button bar.
whyWrong: Sharing is a security configuration, unrelated to action display.
Field requirements come from the field definition or validation.
The highlights panel is governed by the compact layout.

sampleQuestions.question: A designer wants to know how widespread a complaint about navigation is across 4,000 users. Which method is appropriate?
sampleQuestions.explanation: Measuring how many people share an attitude at that scale is what surveys are for.
whyWrong: Usability testing explains specific failures with a handful of participants.
Contextual inquiry is deep observation of a few people in their own setting.
Card sorting informs structure rather than measuring prevalence.

sampleQuestions.question: Which best describes the relationship between the design thinking phases?
options: Iterative: testing can send you back a phase
Strictly sequential, and completed once and for all
sampleQuestions.explanation: The phases loop. Testing frequently sends a team back to redefine the problem or generate new options.
whyWrong: There is a logical order even though teams revisit phases.
Iteration continues after release rather than stopping.
Treating them as a one-way sequence is the common misunderstanding.
